\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Discrete gradient]
\lean{FABL.discreteGradient}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p051-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p222-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p222-b005
}
\label{FABL.discreteGradient}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.discreteDerivative}
Let $f$ be a real-valued function on the $n$-dimensional sign cube, and let $x$ be an
input. The discrete gradient of $f$ at $x$ is the vector in $\bbr^n$ whose coordinate in
direction $i$ is the discrete derivative of $f$ in that direction at $x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Squared norm of the discrete gradient]
\lean{FABL.norm_discreteGradient_sq}
\label{FABL.norm_discreteGradient_sq}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.discreteDerivative, FABL.discreteGradient}
\difficulty{3}
For every nonnegative integer $n$, every real-valued function $f$ on the $n$-dimensional
Boolean cube, and every input $x$, the square of the Euclidean norm of the discrete
gradient of $f$ at $x$ equals the sum over coordinates $i$ of the squared discrete
derivative of $f$ in coordinate $i$ at $x$.
\end{theorem}

total influence is the uniform expectation of the squared Euclidean norm of its discrete

\begin{definition}[Cube Laplacian]

  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p051-b006,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p213-b005

\label{FABL.laplacian}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.coordinateLaplacian}
For each $n\in\mathbb N$, define the Laplacian on real-valued functions on the
$n$-dimensional Boolean cube to be the sum of the coordinate Laplacians over all
coordinates.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Laplacian acting on a function]
\lean{FABL.laplacian_apply}
\label{FABL.laplacian_apply}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.coordinateLaplacian, FABL.laplacian}
\difficulty{1}
For every function $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb R$ and every point $x\in\{-1,1\}^n$, the
Laplacian of $f$ at $x$ is the sum, over all coordinates $i$, of the coordinate
Laplacian of $f$ at $x$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{3}
For every function $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb R$ and every point $x\in\{-1,1\}^n$, $\Delta
f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n (f(x)-f(x^{(i)}))/2$, where $x^{(i)}$ is obtained by flipping
coordinate $i$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{4}
For every function $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb R$ and every point $x\in\{-1,1\}^n$, the
Laplacian satisfies $\Delta f(x)=\frac n2\left(f(x)-\mathbb E_i f(x^{(i)})\right)$,
where $x^{(i)}$ is obtained by flipping coordinate $i$ and the expectation is the
uniform average over coordinates.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{5}
For a Boolean function $f:\{−1,1\}^n\to\{−1,1\}$ and an input $x\in\{−1,1\}^n$, the cube
Laplacian of the real-valued version of $f$ at $x$ equals that value times the number of
coordinates whose flip changes $f(x)$; that is, $\Delta
f(x)=f(x)\,\mathrm{sensitivity}(f,x)$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $f:\\{-1,1\\}^n\\to\\{-1,1\\}$ be any Boolean
function. Its total influence lies in the interval $[0,n]$.
\end{theorem}

Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $f$ be a real-valued function on the
$n$-dimensional sign cube. Its variance is at most its total influence.

\begin{theorem}[Equality of variance and total influence]
\lean{FABL.variance_eq_totalInfluence_iff}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p052-b004}
\label{FABL.variance_eq_totalInfluence_iff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.totalInfluence, FABL.totalInfluence_eq_sum_card_mul_sq_fourierCoeff, FABL.variance, FABL.variance_eq_sum_sq_fourierCoeff}
\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $f$ be a real-valued function on the
$n$-dimensional sign cube. Its variance equals its total influence if and only if every
Fourier coefficient indexed by a subset of more than one coordinate is zero.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $f$ be a real-valued function on the
$n$-dimensional sign cube. Its variance equals its total influence if and only if the
sum of the squared Fourier coefficients indexed by subsets of size at most one equals
the uniform second moment of $f$, namely $\mathbb{E}[f(x)^2]$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, and let $f:\\{-1,1\\}^n\\to\\{-1,1\\}$ depend on at
most one coordinate; that is, there is a set of at most one coordinate on which its
value depends. Then either $f$ is constantly $1$, constantly $-1$, or there is a
coordinate $i$ such that $f(x)=x_i$ for every $x$, or $f(x)=-x_i$ for every $x$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Variance under sign reversal]
\lean{FABL.variance_neg}
\label{FABL.variance_neg}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.mean, FABL.variance}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $f:\{−1,1\}^n\to\mathbb R$. The variance of $-f$
equals the variance of $f$.
\end{theorem}
